items.stem: Exactly one statement below about solving a rational equation is true. Which one is true?
items.hint: Do not judge these by how familiar they look; put one convenient number into each claim and see whether both sides really agree.
worked: Test the splitting claim at $x=4$: $\dfrac{8}{4+4}=1$, but $\dfrac{8}{4}+\dfrac{8}{4}=4$. A fraction never splits over a sum in the denominator.
Test the cancelling claim at $x=3$: $\dfrac{3+3}{3}=2$, not $3$. The $3$ on top is a term, not a factor, so it cannot cancel.
Test the clearing claim on $\dfrac{x}{x-4}=\dfrac{4}{x-4}$: multiplying by $x-4$ gives $x=4$, yet $x=4$ makes both denominators zero, so it solves the cleared equation but not the original.
That last counterexample is exactly why every candidate has to go back into the original equation before it is accepted.

options.text: $\dfrac{8}{x+4}$ may be rewritten as $\dfrac{8}{x}+\dfrac{8}{4}$ before solving.
Once the denominators have been cleared, every root of the resulting equation is a solution of the original equation.
Every candidate root must be substituted into the original equation, because multiplying by the denominator can produce a root that makes a denominator zero.
$\dfrac{x+3}{3}$ may be replaced by $x$ before solving.

items.hint: The two denominators already match, so subtract the numerators over that one denominator, and bracket $5x-4$ before you subtract it.
worked: Multiply both sides by $x-4$: $x^{2}-5x+4=x-4$, so $x^{2}-6x+8=0$ and $(x-2)(x-4)=0$.
Candidates are $x=2$ and $x=4$; reject $x=4$ because it makes the denominator zero.

items.hint: Write down what $x$ is not allowed to be before you clear anything, and remember that a product set equal to $10$ is not a zero-product situation.
worked: The right side is not zero, so expand and move everything over: $x^{2}-x-12=0$, which factors as $(x-4)(x+3)=0$.
Candidates are $x=4$ and $x=-3$; $x=4$ is excluded, so it is extraneous.
